article_title: Everyday Mathematics®
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Spiral curriculum structure: repeated reinforcement of concepts within and across grade levels
description: The curriculum's organizing structure is longitudinal revisiting of content: it "exposes students to material over extended periods of time by repeatedly reinforcing material both within and across grade levels." Program Goals "are organized by content strand and are the same at all grade levels," a structure that "interconnects the curriculum across grades and helps students build a solid base and consistently learn each skill and concept," with Grade-Level Goals specifying the content to master each year.
requirements: A stable set of Program Goals held constant across grade levels, refined into approximately 20–25 Grade-Level Goals per grade, so content can be revisited in varying instructional contexts
target_learning_goals: building a solid base of mathematics skills and concepts consistently across grades
examples: Concepts are reviewed and extended in varying instructional contexts across grade levels; basic skills practice recurs through written and oral fact practice, fluency activities, mental math, daily review problem sets, homework, and math games.

article_title: SpellRead
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: SpellRead™. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Three-phase sequential skill-mastery structure for remedial reading instruction
description: SpellRead™ organizes instruction as "140 lessons implemented in three distinct phases that interweave phonemics, phonetics, and instruction in language-based reading and writing". Phase A (50 lessons) trains the auditory process to hear and manipulate the 44 sounds of English; Phase B (30 lessons) covers secondary vowel spelling, consonant blends, and two-syllable syllabication; Phase C (25 lessons) addresses decoding words of three or more syllables, clusters, and verb forms. Each lesson includes activities for phonemic, phonetic, semantic, syntactic, comprehension/vocabulary, and fluency skills.
requirements: Systematic and explicit instruction with specific skill mastery emphasized
Small-group delivery with one instructor
target_learners: Struggling readers in grades 2 or above
target_learning_goals: Phonemic awareness
Decoding and word attack
Multisyllabic word reading
Reading fluency and comprehension
examples: Phase A (50 lessons) is designed to train the auditory process function of the brain to hear and manipulate the 44 sounds of the English language

citation: Yuchen Liu, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Riordan Alfredo, Paola Mejia-Domenzain, Dwi Rahayu, and Sadia Nawaz. (2026). AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09831
title: Spatial pedagogy framework of four classroom space types
description: Spatial pedagogy is a theoretical lens holding that "classroom spaces acquire pedagogical meaning through the discourse enacted at particular physical classroom areas, as well as through teachers' positioning and proximity to students and learning resources". It distinguishes four space types — Authoritative, Interactional, Supervisory, and Personal — characterised through observable spatial pedagogy behaviours. The article applies it to team-teaching contexts, where multiple teachers share and negotiate classroom space, and refines the Interactional type into talk-oriented categories for its coding scheme.
requirements: Requires structured classroom observation of teachers' positioning and movement, and, to capture enactment fully, analysis of how teachers speak within these spaces, since the same spatial configuration can serve different instructional purposes
constraints: The article notes spatial positioning alone is insufficient to fully capture enactment because pedagogical meaning is also shaped by how teachers speak within these spaces
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate university students in team-taught classes
target_learning_goals: understanding and describing the micro-level enactment of teaching in classroom space
examples: The study coded spatial pedagogy behaviours in 36 team-teaching sessions using a scheme adapted from this framework, retaining Instruction, Interaction and Collaboration categories

article_title: Generative AI May Reinforce Social Biases in Software Engineering Education
citation: Erfan Entezami, Andrew Lan, and Madeline Endres. (2026). Generative AI May Reinforce Social Biases in Software Engineering Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28483
title: When deploying LLMs for educational decision-making, explicitly specify decision criteria and minimize unnecessary demographic cues
description: The article's mitigation principle is that prompt design and the information provided to a model substantially influence its biased behavior. It recommends that practitioners "explicitly specify the criteria used to make decisions and minimize unnecessary demographic cues", because seemingly innocuous attributes such as names signaling gender or nationality can affect model outputs. The study's persona experiments show that adding task-relevant skill information reduced but did not eliminate bias, supporting information design as a partial mitigation lever.
requirements: Instructors or practitioners must know which attributes (e.g., names) may implicitly signal demographic characteristics before submitting student information to the model.
constraints: The article shows additional task-relevant information reduced biases but did not fully eliminate them; demographic attributes still influenced decisions when multiple valid options existed.
target_learners: software engineering students in team-based courses
target_learning_goals: fair and equitable team formation and educational content generation
examples: In the team formation experiments, Skill-based personas containing technical qualifications steered assignments toward ground-truth teams (99.2% on-pair) yet gender still biased the choice between equally valid teams.

article_title: Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI
citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Lisa Siegrist, Niklas Scholz, Shintaro Sato, Martina Vincoli, and Man Su. 2026. Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI. Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. 10, 6, Article CSCW124. https://doi.org/10.1145/3816972
title: Speed-dating storyboard method with pair-matching analysis for eliciting multi-stakeholder views on classroom AI
description: The study used a qualitative speed-dating method in which 16 students and 15 teachers in Germany individually reacted to eight storyboards (five scenes each, with positive and negative endings) about AI use in classrooms, presented in random order with guiding questions. Sessions lasted about 45 to 60 minutes and produced roughly 14.0 hours of student recordings and 17.4 hours of teacher recordings. Open coding yielded 644 student and 637 teacher codes; Affinity Diagramming produced low-level themes, and a pair-matching analysis across 438 individual low-level themes yielded 55 matched pairs, grouped into 11 mid-level and five high-level themes. Storyboards are available on OSF.

Student and teacher versions of scenarios should depict identical situations from each stakeholder's point of view
constraints: Conducted in Germany, where few participants had used AI-based learning systems, and the authors note the German school context may differ from other educational contexts
The authors state they did not use inter-rater reliability statistics or predefined coding schemes, following Affinity Diagramming conventions
target_learning_goals: Eliciting stakeholder preferences and (mis)alignments regarding student versus AI decision-making control
examples: A storyboard on AI-based automatic group assignment showed a positive ending (effective collaboration) and a negative ending (teacher unable to change grouping despite a student's request)

article_title: From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education
citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: Spoke-and-Wheel teaching architecture: three quantum-specialist agents in parallel coordinated by a Synthesizer
description: ITAS's teaching architecture decomposes tutoring by task: three specialist agents (Video, Guidance, Code) analyze each student question in parallel, each reasoning only within its designated scope, and a Synthesizer Agent integrates their outputs using a priority hierarchy with code errors first, then conceptual gaps, then video references. The design responds to the prototype's task-boundary hallucinations, which the authors attribute to cognitive overload of a single overloaded agent. Specialization is said to reduce hallucination via cognitive load reduction, task interference elimination, and synthesis filtering. The three-agent count "emerged empirically; two agents conflated code and concepts, while four added coordination overhead without reliability improvement."
requirements: Each agent must carry quantum-specific domain knowledge, e.g. a timestamp-indexed concept map for the Video Agent and a hand-curated Qiskit error catalog for the Code Agent
constraints: A controlled, blinded comparison against the prototype on the same input set remains future work
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum information science
Qiskit implementation skills
video lecture comprehension
examples: A student question about a QiskitError applying Pauli-Z was handled by parallel Video, Code, and Guidance agent analyses synthesized into one response addressing video context, code diagnosis, and conceptual confirmation

article_title: Special-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Special Education — Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training
citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Special-R1: disability-aware pedagogical RL coupling a two-dimensional adaptive prompt with a persona-aware Thinking Reward
description: Special-R1 is a framework extending pedagogical multi-turn RL to special education. It factors pedagogical support into two orthogonal dimensions: a support level (amount) mapped from the learner's baseline accuracy to Maximum, Moderate, or Minimum support following the I-Do / We-Do / You-Do progression, and a support style (manner) drawn from the learner's disability profile, so that "thewhatcomes from the support level, thehowcomes from the disability profile." Its second component is a persona-aware Thinking Reward whose judge is prompted with the learner's disability profile and scores whether the thinking trace reflects disability-appropriate reasoning, which the authors describe as "the first reward we are aware of that explicitly scoresdisability-appropriatereasoning."
requirements: Requires a pre-measured baseline accuracy of the student simulator on the given problem type to select the support level, and a structured disability rubric with learning characteristics, communication patterns, and recommended tutor strategies.
constraints: Every student in the framework is a disability-conditioned LLM simulator; improvements on judge-based metrics have not been validated with real learners with disabilities.
Experiments use 7-8B tutors; behavior at larger scales remains to be studied.
target_learners: Learners with disabilities across five profiles: intellectual disability, specific learning disability, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and emotional/behavioral disorder
target_learning_goals: Multi-domain tutoring covering mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, and life skills
examples: The adaptive prompt maps baseline accuracy in [0.01, 0.20) to Maximum support (micro-steps, concrete examples), [0.20, 0.40) to Moderate support, and [0.40, 0.60) to Minimum support with open-ended questions.
key_sources: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670

citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Released Special-R1 artifacts: multi-domain ZPD-filtered corpus, SPED-Tutor-Mix evaluation set, seven checkpoints, and disability-aware evaluation pipeline
description: The article releases the training and evaluation artifacts behind Special-R1. The evaluation set is the persona-augmented SPED-Tutor-Mix test split in which "every item carries a disability profile so that persona-aware metrics can be computed." The disability rubric is released as disability_types.yaml alongside the code, together with all seven model checkpoints and the evaluation pipeline.

constraints: The corpus contains a comparatively small number of LD-appropriate mathematics items, which the authors link to the sld_math weakness.

target_learning_goals: Multi-domain tutoring: mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, and life skills
examples: Mathematics contributes roughly 11k problems after filtering (GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, BigMath subset); social reasoning contributes roughly 29k (SocialIQA); 5% of the filtered corpus is held out as the in-domain test set.

article_title: Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication
citation: Ching-Jung Cheng, Yu-Chan Chung, Bing-Chen Chiu, Yu-Hsuan Lin, and Jia-Wei Liao. 2026. Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication: A Probe-Grounded Co-Design Study. OzCHI '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07503
title: Spritz: a Discord-based LLM technology probe for AI-mediated interdisciplinary team communication
description: Spritz is a Discord-based AI conversational agent designed as a technology probe for interdisciplinary team communication, "enabling participants to reflect on the role, value, and boundaries of AI mediation rather than evaluating a mature system". It monitors shared-channel messages for semantic and pragmatic tensions, pauses the discussion, elicits individual perspectives in private channels, and returns anonymized syntheses to the group. In the study, four three-person groups completed a 15-minute resource-allocation discussion, with an average of two detected tension episodes per session.
requirements: Its design was guided by three goals: detecting potential collaboration tensions, supporting members in articulating implicit reasoning through private reflection, and helping the group compare alternative perspectives through anonymized synthesis
constraints: Detection used a fixed 0.7 confidence threshold and a ten-message trigger that were design choices for the exploratory probe and were not empirically calibrated; the authors state they do not know how accurately Spritz detected boundaries under this configuration
target_learners: university students in interdisciplinary project teams
target_learning_goals: negotiating disciplinary differences in text-based collaborative problem-solving
examples: Four groups of three students role-played technical, business, and UX members allocating 10 resource points across fixing defects, refining the business narrative, and user research while Spritz mediated

article_title: Practical Implementation Report on Introducing Spec-Driven Development Using AI Agents in Software Development PBL
citation: Hidetake Tanaka, Hiroshi Igaki, Kazumasa Shimari, Kiyoshi Honda, and Naoki Fukuyasu. (2026). Practical Implementation Report on Introducing Spec-Driven Development Using AI Agents in Software Development PBL. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30572
title: Spec-Driven Development (SDD): a development methodology in which AI agents generate code from structured specification documents that developers must verify
description: SDD is a software development methodology proposed for use with AI agents, positioned as an alternative to Vibe Coding. "This approach involves deﬁning detailed speciﬁcations cl early at the early stages of development and having AI agents gener ate code based on those speciﬁcations." Its distinguishing feature is that agents proceed from structured specification documents rather than ambiguous natural-language instructions, with specifications describing architectural patterns, coding conventions, security requirements, and testing strategies that agents treat as constraints. Because developers must understand and verify the generated documents and code, the authors judge SDD more suitable than Vibe Coding for project-based courses where students take responsibility for AI outputs.
requirements: Developers must understand and verify AI-generated specifications and documents at each step to maintain code quality and consistency
constraints: SDD demands greater expertise compared to Vibe Coding, per the authors
target_learning_goals: application development skills
understanding and verifying AI-generated specifications and code
examples: In the SDPBL course, the existing SDD requirements-analysis and design phases were redefined as an investigation phase, and a review phase was added after implementation, yielding a four-phase workflow

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Specify-Predict-Delegate-Verify-Interpret workflow for AI-era computational work
description: The article organizes its five pillars into a repeating workflow: "Specify → Predict → Delegate → Verify → Interpret; Iterate." Students specify the problem, inputs, outputs, and physical model; predict the result before any execution as a Fermi estimate; delegate execution to the tool; verify output against the prediction; interpret physically and iterate. The author argues a student who has committed to an expectation is testing a hypothesis when the plot appears, while one who has not is merely looking at a picture. Calibrated reliance—knowing how much verification is owed for this tool on this task—threads through the loop.
requirements: Prediction must be made before execution, without the tool, so the later verification has a committed expectation to test against.
constraints: The required verification depth scales with the tool: a calculator needs a glance, a community-validated library routine interface-level checks, a bespoke agent-generated simulation the full battery every time.
target_learning_goals: orchestrating AI-assisted computational work with verification and physical interpretation
examples: The article's supplementary progression walks tasks from single-digit addition to agent-orchestrated molecular dynamics, recording at each rung what the era's tool absorbs and what remains human.
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis.
citation: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354
title: Distributed practice framework distinguishing spacing effects from lag effects
description: The article organizes the distributed practice literature around temporal variables it defines explicitly: interstudy interval (ISI), the interval separating study episodes of the same material, and retention interval, the interval between the last study episode and the final test. It distinguishes the spacing effect, "enhanced learning during spaced as compared with massed study episodes for a given item," from the lag effect, comparisons of different levels of spacing, and treats distributed practice as the generic term encompassing both. This distinction proved, in the authors' words, helpful in quantifying how retention depends jointly on ISI and retention interval.
requirements: Studies must include at least two learning episodes per item, or one massed presentation with lag under 1 s, and a recall final test
constraints: The review is restricted to verbal memory tasks using recall as the performance measure, excluding recognition and frequency-judgment measures and clinical populations
target_learners: learners of verbal information across ages, including children and older adults
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of verbal material

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention
citation: Latimier, A., Peyre, H., & Ramus, F. (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8
title: Spaced retrieval practice as the combination of two desirable difficulties
description: The article defines spaced retrieval practice as a learning strategy in which "repetitions of the same retrieval event [are] distributed through time". It frames this strategy as combining two desirable difficulties: retrieval practice and the spacing effect. The framework organises the meta-analysis into two questions — spaced versus massed retrieval practice, and expanding versus uniform spacing schedules — and positions spacing of retrieval episodes as the mechanism by which final retention is enhanced.
requirements: Learning episodes must involve actual retrieval events on the same content, distributed through time, for the strategy to apply as defined
constraints: The benefit concerns final retention of the same content; the article finds no support for progressively increasing inter-retrieval intervals until the retention test
target_learners: learners across the 29 included studies, spanning classroom and laboratory settings
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied content
examples: The meta-analysis operationalised the framework by dividing 29 studies into subset 1 (spaced vs massed retrieval) and subset 2 (expanding vs uniform schedules)

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention
citation: Latimier, A., Peyre, H., & Ramus, F. (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8
title: Space out retrieval practice episodes on the same content, but do not assume intervals must progressively expand
description: The article's overall conclusion is that "these results support the advantage of spacing out the retrieval practice episodes on the same content, but do not support the widely held belief that inter-retrieval intervals should be progressively increased until a retention test". Designers should therefore distribute retrieval practice over time, while uniform spacing schedules perform as well as expanding ones overall. The expanding schedule's advantage appears only when items are tested many times.
requirements: Retrieval practice episodes must target the same content and be distributed through time rather than massed
constraints: Progressively increasing inter-retrieval intervals is not supported overall; the expanding schedule only becomes more beneficial than the uniform one as the number of exposures increases
target_learners: students in classroom and laboratory learning settings
target_learning_goals: final retention of learned content
examples: The review aggregated 39 effect sizes for the spaced-versus-massed contrast and 54 for the expanding-versus-uniform contrast to reach this recommendation

article_title: Guidance during mathematical problem solving.
citation: Ahmad Tarmizi, Rohani. (1991). Guidance During Mathematical Problem Solving. Doctoral thesis, University of New South Wales. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/69310
title: Split-attention cognitive load account of guidance effects
description: The thesis explains its experimental results through cognitive load and attention: guidance such as worked examples normally reduces load and directs attention appropriately, helping schema acquisition. However, domains like geometry require learners to "mentally integrate multiple sources of information, resulting in splitting of attention", which raises load and eliminates the guidance benefit. Presenting information in a unitary format removes the split, restoring the worked-example advantage.
requirements: Guidance material must avoid requiring learners to mentally integrate multiple, physically separated sources of information for the benefit to appear
constraints: The benefit of worked examples and similar guidance is eliminated in areas such as geometry where multiple sources must be integrated and attention is split
target_learning_goals: acquisition of problem-solving schemas in mathematics and science
examples: Circle geometry problems in which text and diagram were first separated (splitting attention) and then presented in a unitary, integrated format across Experiments 1-5

article_title: The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development
citation: Thomas C. Toppino and William DiGeorge. (1984). The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development. Memory & Cognition, 12(2), 118-122. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+spacing+effect+in+free+recall+emerges+with+development+Memory+%26+Cognition+1984
title: Deficient-processing and encoding-variability theories of the spacing effect
description: The article organizes spacing-effect explanations into two major categories. Deficient-processing theories explain "poor memory for massed repetitions" by assuming one presentation is not fully processed, with processing increasing as spacing grows; encoding-variability theories hold that "repetition facilitates mem­ory to the extent that each presentation is encoded differently, thereby establishing more ways to access the information at retrieval." The authors evaluate both categories against their developmental findings.
requirements: An adequate general account must incorporate processes that become active later in childhood rather than relying solely on automatic encoding processes operative from early infancy
constraints: The authors state that encoding variability theories are often vague about whether variable encoding is involuntary or the result of voluntary strategies
target_learning_goals: memory for repeated information in free recall
examples: The authors judge the voluntary-attention deficient-processing theory most compatible with their results, assuming the strategy of not fully processing the second occurrence of a massed repetition develops between roughly ages 4 and 6
key_sources: Thomas C. Toppino and William DiGeorge. (1984). The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development. Memory & Cognition, 12(2), 118-122. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+spacing+effect+in+free+recall+emerges+with+development+Memory+%26+Cognition+1984

article_title: The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development
citation: Thomas C. Toppino and William DiGeorge. (1984). The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development. Memory & Cognition, 12(2), 118-122. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+spacing+effect+in+free+recall+emerges+with+development+Memory+%26+Cognition+1984
title: Accounts of the spacing effect must include processes acquired or developed during childhood, not only hard-wired mechanisms
description: The article argues that because the spacing effect in free recall is absent in preschoolers but present in first-graders, explanations "cannot rely solely on automatic encoding processes that are operative from early infancy, but must incorpo­rate processes that become active later in childhood." Any hard-wired mechanism suggested by infant recognition data may be limited to recognition memory, with free recall depending on developed or acquired processes.
requirements: An adequate account must explain why the spacing effect emerges between approximately ages 4 and 6
constraints: If a primitive mechanism underlies the spacing effect in free recall, it is apparently not sufficient to produce the phenomenon until augmented by other developing processes
target_learning_goals: memory for repeated information
examples: The authors propose that a voluntary strategy of diverting attention from the second occurrence of massed repetitions may be acquired between ages 4 and 6, consistent with the developmental trend for attention to become increasingly active and directed

article_title: Physical Activity and Cognitive Functioning of Children: A Systematic Review
citation: Bidzan-Bluma Ilona, Lipowska Małgorzata. (2018). Physical Activity and Cognitive Functioning of Children: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15040800
title: Model of the influence of sport on children's physical, mental, and social resources
description: The authors developed a model, presented in Figure 2, outlining how sport influences three resource domains in children in late childhood: physical resources (e.g., physical fitness, motor skills), mental resources (cognitive functioning, executive functions, motivation, ability to set goals, self-control, and emotional functioning), and social resources (e.g., social support, fostering positive values, and etiquette). The model holds that these results are relevant "independent of whether the physical activity is unorganized free play or organized activity, such as for a sports club and school activities". It synthesizes the review's findings across attention, thinking, language, learning, and memory.
requirements: Based on the review's included studies of physical activity and cognition in children; the authors built it on prior models (McMorris et al.; Diehl et al.)
constraints: Developed from a review whose included studies were limited in number, cultural balance, and methodological quality, per the authors' own limitations section
target_learning_goals: cognitive functioning, executive functions, emotional functioning, social values
examples: The review's Figure 2 depicts the model of sport's influence on physical, mental, and social resources, developed by the authors.

article_title: Neural bases of orthographic long-term memory and working memory in dysgraphia
citation: Rapp, Brenda; Purcell, Jeremy; Hillis, Argye; Capasso, Rita; Miceli, Gabriele. (2016). Neural bases of orthographic long-term memory and working memory in dysgraphia. BRAIN. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awv348
title: Two-component architecture of spelling: orthographic long-term memory retrieval plus working-memory maintenance before serial motor production
description: The article frames spelling as a multi-component process: information about a word's letters and their order is retrieved from long-term memory, then maintained and processed by working memory in preparation for serial production by the motor system. The article states that "Spelling a word involves the retrieval of information about the word's letters and their order from long-term memory as well as the maintenance and processing of this information by working memory in preparation for serial production by the motor system." This architecture motivates distinguishing dysgraphia forms that selectively affect each component.
requirements: Spelling performance must be interpretable as depending on separable orthographic long-term memory and working memory processes
constraints: The framework is stated for written word production (spelling), not other language tasks
target_learners: adults learning or relearning written spelling
target_learning_goals: spelling
retrieval of letter identities and order
written word production
examples: The study classified 27 individuals with deficits affecting only one of the two processes and 6 with deficits affecting both

article_title: Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study
citation: Yılmaz, E., Yel, S., & Griffiths, M. D. (2022). Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104548
title: Social Problem Situations Inventory for Children (SPSIC)
description: The SPSIC (Yılmaz et al., 2021) measures children's social problem-solving skills across "six dimensions (impulse control, communication, cooperation, social initiation, empathy, and emotion regulation)", each with a social problem situation. Children follow four solution steps (defining the problem, producing solutions, identifying the most effective solution and explaining the reason), each scored 0-4 by two coders, for a maximum of 16 points per scenario and 96 overall.
requirements: Responses coded by two trained coders with an experienced third researcher consulted on disagreements
constraints: The best solution chosen could not be tested in the school setting, so children explained why their chosen solution was best
target_learning_goals: social problem-solving skills

article_title: Specific Retrieval Deficit from Long-Term Memory in Children with Poor Arithmetic Facts Abilities
citation: Mussolin, C. and Noël, M-P. (2008). Specific Retrieval Deficit from Long-Term Memory in Children with Poor Arithmetic Facts Abilities. The Open Psychology Journal. https://doi.org/10.2174/1874350100801010026
title: Specific numerical retrieval deficit hypothesis: arithmetic fact retrieval difficulties in MD reflect a deficit specific to the numerical semantic system
description: The article proposes that children with mathematical disorders have a deficit specific to the retrieval of arithmetic facts from long-term memory, rather than a general speed-of-processing, semantic memory, or verbal routine deficit. The authors state that "the difficulties in the retrieval of numbers and arithmetic facts encountered by children with MD could not be attributed to a general deficit in speed of access or to a deficit with verbal material in general, but seem to be specific to the semantic system of numbers." This account aligns with Butterworth's defective number module hypothesis and Dehaene's number sense deficit hypothesis.
requirements: Requires contrasting performance across multiple retrieval tasks tapping different cognitive domains to isolate the numerical specificity of the deficit.
constraints: The article notes it remains open whether PoorAF children used retrieval strategies rather than counting, and whether the deficit reflects access or storage.
target_learners: children with poor arithmetic fact abilities
target_learning_goals: retrieval of basic arithmetic facts from long-term memory
examples: The study compared 18 PoorAF children to 18 matched controls across six computerized selection tasks, finding slowing only in the multiplication task.

article_title: Metacognition in Later Adulthood
citation: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/
title: Use spared metacognitive monitoring as the basis for compensatory self-regulated learning in older adults
description: The article argues that because aging spares monitoring accuracy, "spared monitoring is available as a resource that older adults can use to improve their learning." Older adults who accurately monitor what they have and have not learned can allocate restudy effort selectively to unlearned items, compensating for age-related declines in learning mechanisms. This principle underlies the article's metacognitive intervention program and its recommendation that monitoring-informed self-regulation supports everyday cognitive functioning.
requirements: Individuals must be able to monitor their learning accurately, e.g., via self-testing akin to making highly accurate delayed JOLs
Study must afford differential allocation of time and effort to unlearned items, e.g., self-paced study
constraints: Training metacognitive self-regulation without explicit transfer discussion showed no transfer to a different kind of memory task, free recall of word lists
target_learning_goals: compensating for age-related memory declines
achieving satisfactory levels of final learning through selective restudy
examples: The Dunlosky et al. (2003) intervention trained older individuals to self-test and focus restudy on unlearned items, producing greater improvements than encoding-strategy training under self-paced study

article_title: Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes
citation: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y
title: Specific (splitting) models assume different types of adversity confer distinct effects on separable neural systems
description: The review describes specific or splitting models as a reaction to cumulative models, based on the premise that different types of adversity each confer specific effects, and links to neurobiological or cognitive systems may be masked by heterogeneous samples. An increasingly prevalent variant conceptualizes potential stressors as a lack of expected inputs (deprivation, including neglect, food deprivation, and institutionalization) or a presence of direct threat to the child (threat, including physical abuse, sexual abuse, and exposure to violence). These approaches are grounded in animal models demonstrating some specificity in the effects of certain types of stressors on neurobiological systems.
requirements: Assessment approaches that distinguish types or dimensions of adversity, such as deprivation versus threat, rather than summing heterogeneous events
constraints: The review notes different types of stressors often co-occur, creating conceptual issues and making it difficult to determine if one specific type or dimension of stressor is driving an effect
target_learners: children exposed to chronic or extreme stress in early life
target_learning_goals: identifying the distinct neurobiological mechanisms linking specific types of early adversity to development
examples: The review cites work conceptualizing stressors as deprivation (neglect, food deprivation, institutionalization) versus threat (physical abuse, sexual abuse, exposure to violence)

article_title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
citation: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z
title: Specify behaviors carefully if a leader role is assigned to collaborative groups
description: The article's abstract and findings indicate that because leadership naturally splits into intellectual and organizational components taken by different students, "care should be taken to specify behaviors if the roleof leader is assigned to collaborative groups." Assigning a single undifferentiated leader role risks loading one student with behaviors that naturally distribute across members, so any assigned role should spell out which leadership behaviors it covers.
requirements: If a leader role is assigned, the specific behaviors expected of that role must be specified rather than leaving a single generic leader role.
constraints: The recommendation derives from observed emergent patterns in year-six groups on mystery tasks; the article did not experimentally test assigned leader roles.
target_learners: primary school students in collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: effective role assignment in collaborative group work
examples: The article contrasts instructor-managed participation via assigned roles or scripts with groups managing their own participation, motivating the examination of emergent leadership.

article_title: It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice
citation: Tino Endres, Lena Kranzdorf, Vivien Schneider, Alexander Renkl. (2020). It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09526-1
title: Spreading activation account of task-specific retrieval practice effects
description: The article draws on elaborative retrieval theory, in which recalling specific knowledge strengthens that memory trace and search processes "spreads activation to other pieces of knowledge that are connected to the retrieved piece of knowledge". Task specificity shapes the activation pattern: specific short-answer tasks strongly activate targeted pieces, while free-recall distributes activation across many pieces. The authors argue this account has "greater explanatory value than the transfer-appropriate processing perspective" for differences among recall tasks.
requirements: Learning materials must contain meaningful cues connecting knowledge pieces, which the authors assume present in complex learning
constraints: The authors state their study was not designed to (dis-)confirm theories and that follow-up studies should test the spreading-activation assumption
target_learning_goals: retention of expository text content
examples: The study differentiated targeted versus non-targeted content sections when assessing delayed learning outcomes, enabling fine-grained tests of activation-pattern predictions

article_title: Scrum methodology in context-based secondary chemistry classes: effects on students’ achievement and on students’ perceptions of affective and metacognitive dimensions of their learning
citation: Vogelzang, J., Admiraal, W. F., van Driel, J. H. (2021). title: Sprint-structured context-based learning cycle alternating performing and evaluating phases with systematic check moments

The comparison group worked collaboratively with "no systematic check moments on conceptual development or quality of learning process". Within the experimental group "a continuous alternation of performing and evaluating is found, whereas the performing phase and evaluating phase are separated in the comparison group".

reflection on learning strategies

article_title: Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition
citation: Demian Scherer, Annika Verkühlen, Stephan Dutke. (2023). Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09618-8
title: Spreading activation account of related-picture effects: passive mutual facilitation of related concepts improves encoding into long-term memory
description: The article proposes that thematically related non-explanatory pictures improve learning through spreading activation: in semantic networks "activation can spread back and forth between related concepts", so related concepts "mutually reactivate each other", which automatically maintains related information in working memory longer and increases the probability of encoding into long-term memory (drawing on Davelaar et al., 2006, and Anderson's spreading activation theories). Because the process is passive, effects should appear mainly on retention/knowledge measures rather than transfer. The two experiments' pattern — knowledge gains in Experiment 1, metacognitive monitoring gains in Experiment 2, no transfer effects — is interpreted as consistent with this account.
requirements: Pictures must be related to the text's content without directly representing or explaining the text's main concepts, so effects cannot be attributed to explanatory power or dual coding redundancy
constraints: The effect is predicted to appear on knowledge/retention measures, not necessarily transfer, "because of the passive nature of the spreading activation process"
In Experiment 1 the monitoring effect did not appear, so the account does not predict which of the two knowledge-derived measures manifests the benefit
target_learners: university students in teacher education seminars
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition from expository text
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: Experiment 1 pictures included a library photo related to study behavior and a mountain runner related to the effort assumption of self-control; the text described abstract concepts (willpower, population growth) that pictures could not directly represent

article_title: Do specific relevance instructions promote transfer appropriate processing?
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden. (2011). Do specific relevance instructions promote transfer appropriate processing? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9158-x
title: Give learners specific pre-reading relevance instructions to shape the quality of memory for text
description: This principle holds that telling learners, before reading, the specific questions their reading should address (e.g., what-questions or why-questions) directs processing toward those questions and improves later recall of matching information. The study found participants "did better on questions that had greater similarity to relevance instructions", consistent with transfer appropriate processing.

constraints: The recall advantage applies to test questions similar to the instruction; control readers recalled equal amounts across question types

article_title: Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z
title: Specialized purpose hypothesis: each type of engagement has its own specialized function targeted toward a specific purpose
description: The article proposes and tests the specialized purpose hypothesis, namely that each type of engagement has its own specialized function targeted toward a specific purpose, such as to boost achievement, social support, motivation, or well-being. As illustrated in Fig. 1, it assigns behavioral engagement primarily to achievement, agentic engagement to recruiting social support, cognitive engagement to achievement and cognition-based motivations, and emotional engagement to well-being and need-based motivations. The four meta-analyses were designed to test whether one type of engagement predicts each correlate more strongly than the others.

constraints: The article notes the findings raise challenging questions about how to better conceptualize and measure each type of engagement

social support
motivation
well-being

article_title: A New Perspective on Perspective Taking: A Multidimensional Approach to Conceptualizing an Aptitude
citation: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2004). A New Perspective on Perspective Taking: A Multidimensional Approach to Conceptualizing an Aptitude. Educational Psychology Review 16 (3). https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034021.12899.11
title: SPT as a multidimensional, situated aptitude with commitment and performance pathways
description: The article applies Snow's situated aptitude theory to social perspective taking, defining aptitude as the "degree of readiness to learn and to perform well in a particular situation or in a fixed domain". SPT aptitude has two pathways: a commitment pathway whose outcome is SPT propensity (how frequently students attempt perspective taking) and a performance pathway whose outcome is SPT ability (accuracy of inferring others' thoughts and feelings). Aptitudes develop through these pathways coalescing into an aptitude complex, and interact with a layered problem space of task and context.
requirements: Assessment of both propensity and ability simultaneously, since each pathway has a distinct measurable outcome
constraints: The article divides the situation into task-level and contextual-level factors only, omitting Snow's treatment layer because SPT is rarely taught in schools

conflict resolution

title: Taxonomy of personal and situational factors affecting SPT propensity and accuracy
description: The article organizes research and hypotheses into a taxonomy summarized in Tables 1 and 2, structured so that moving left to right, perspective taking should be facilitated by increasing propensity and/or accuracy. Person-level factors include motivation and emotion regulation (commitment pathway) and cognitive level, strategy, and cognitive style (performance pathway). As the article states, "Students' SPT propensity and accuracy will vary according to seven aspects of these tasks: locus, decipherability, familiarity, temporality, reality, duration, and morality", plus two contextual features, cooperativeness and distractions.
requirements: Future studies should relate cognitive style to SPT propensity while controlling for gender and ethnicity, per the article's own methodological recommendation
constraints: Many cells of the taxonomy are explicitly hypothetical; the article notes no research has examined several associations, such as familiarity's effect on propensity

interpersonal understanding

article_title: A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education
citation: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z
title: Classify a spatial factor only if it concerns visual stimuli, is uninfluenced by semantic knowledge, and is theoretically separable from existing factors
description: The article establishes inclusion and exclusion criteria for calling a factor a spatial factor, because factor names do not always align across studies and knowledge-laden factors have been misclassified. It states that "the criteria used to identify factors as spatial factors are that they are mental abilities concerned specifically with visual stimuli and which are not influenced by semantic knowledge", and that newly identified factors must at minimum be theoretically separable from existing factors. This guards against misrepresenting knowledge-dependent performance as spatial cognition.
requirements: Test instruments may require contextual adaptations, but their capacity to validly identify a unique factor should not be compromised; semantic knowledge must not dictate access to the cognitive resources
constraints: Factors describing feelings, fixation periods, or knowledge-reliant tasks (e.g. geographic knowledge in the Spatial Thinking Ability Test) do not qualify as spatial factors
target_learners: STEM education researchers designing studies of spatial factors
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification and measurement of spatial factors in educational research
examples: The article excludes Roff's maintenance-of-contact and effect-of-uncertainty factors and flags Lee and Bednarz's spatial thinking components as relying on geographic knowledge rather than qualifying as spatial factors.

article_title: The Social Side of School: Why Teachers Need Social Psychology
citation: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2010). The social side of school: Why teachers need social psychology. Educational Psychology Review 22, no. 3: 349-362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9138-3
title: Social perspective taking as a two-dimensional aptitude with ability and motivational components
description: The review presents social perspective taking (SPT) as the construct of "discerning the thoughts and feelings of others with particular attention to how others perceive the situation." Following Gehlbach (2004), it characterizes SPT as "a complex aptitude, consisting of an ability dimension as well as a motivational dimension," so that real-world impact requires both accurate reading of others and motivation to engage frequently. The review proposes that teachers' SPT, once biases are mitigated, can improve monitoring of student progress and pedagogy.
requirements: For SPT to impact outcomes in the real world, people need both the ability to read thoughts and feelings accurately and the motivation to engage in SPT frequently
constraints: The review notes that little of the bias research has focused specifically on teachers, presuming they are as susceptible as anyone else
target_learning_goals: accurately perceiving students' thoughts, feelings, and motivations to improve pedagogy and monitoring of student progress
examples: A science teacher used SPT to anticipate where chemistry students struggled due to their non-analytic, sequential way of thinking, tailoring lessons and reading facial expressions to gauge comprehension

article_title: Sex Differences in Mathematics: A Meta-analytic Review Across Content, Grades, and Geographic Regions
citation: Sara Caviola, David Giofrè, Enrico Toffalini, Lorenzo Esposito, Irene Tonizzi, David C. Geary. (2026). Sex Differences in Mathematics: A Meta-analytic Review Across Content, Grades, and Geographic Regions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10125-8
title: Spatial-ability account of content- and grade-specific sex differences in mathematics
description: The article organizes its findings around an explanatory framework in which sex differences in mathematics are content- and grade-specific because mathematical domains differ in their reliance on visuospatial abilities. It notes that boys' advantage in spatial abilities increases from childhood into adolescence, and that mathematical domains influenced by spatial abilities, such as geometry, show correspondingly growing male advantages. The framework also incorporates socio-cultural factors, including mathematics anxiety and stereotype-related mechanisms, and school practices such as tracking and course placement that may mitigate or amplify gaps.
requirements: Distinguishing mathematics content by its visuospatial component and relating domain-specific gaps to developmental trajectories of spatial abilities
constraints: The article states the findings do not mean boys have advantages in all aspects of geometry, such as writing geometric proofs, but only content involving active manipulation of visuospatial information
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance across content domains and grade levels
examples: The article links the growing geometry advantage to boys' increasing spatial-ability advantage from childhood into adolescence

article_title: Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses
citation: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
title: Spacing effect as a cognitive load effect: working memory resource depletion during learning with recovery during rest-from-deliberate-learning
description: The review proposes that the spacing effect is a cognitive load effect: continuous mental effort depletes limited working memory resources, depressing subsequent performance, and rest-from-deliberate-learning periods allow those resources to be restored, enhancing later learning. The authors state that "CLT assumes that inserted spacing with rest-from-deliberate-learning during spaced practice allows the restoration of depleted working memory resources, thus enhancing subsequent learning." Unlike most cognitive load effects, this one does not require high element interactivity materials.
requirements: A rest-from-deliberate-learning period between learning episodes during which intentional learning does not occur
constraints: The article notes it is not known whether depletion is greater with high than low element interactivity information
Only Chen et al. (2018) directly assessed working memory resources; the authors are not aware of other studies that did
target_learners: students across all stages of education
target_learning_goals: retention and learning outcomes across verbal, motor, and academic domains
examples: Chen et al. (2018) administered a working memory capacity test immediately before the content test to massed and spaced groups, finding recovery after rest associated with superior learning

citation: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
title: Use spaced instruction when learners need mental rest and interleaved instruction when learners must discriminate between similar areas
description: From the review's practical conclusion, the two effects call for different instructional conditions: spacing supports learning when gaps provide genuine rest from deliberate learning, while interleaving supports learning when learners must learn to tell apart apparently similar but different topics. The authors state: "Spacing should be used when learners need to mentally rest from learning while interleaving should be used when learners need to discriminate between apparently similar but in fact different instructional areas."

constraints: Interleaving with obviously different materials or knowledgeable learners is unlikely to produce an effect, per the five null studies
target_learners: students across all stages of education
target_learning_goals: retention of learned material and discrimination between similar concepts or problem types
examples: The review's coding classified 48 studies as spacing (with rest) and 67 as interleaving (without rest), including lag designs as interleaving

article_title: Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning
citation: Keith B. Lyle, Campbell R. Bego, Patricia A. S. Ralston, Jason C. Immekus. (2022). Spaced Retrieval Practice Imposes Desirable Difficulty in Calculus Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09677-2
title: Distribute calculus practice across multiple quizzes and accept lower short-term practice performance for better long-term retention
description: Because spacing improved end-of-semester test scores while reducing practice-quiz performance, the article recommends that instructors distribute quiz questions on a learning objective across several quizzes rather than presenting all variants on one quiz. The authors "encourage instructors and students alike to embrace the short-term pain of spacing in order to reap its long-term gain", noting spacing is a low- or no-cost intervention requiring no increase in the amount of work assigned. Practice performance alone is a misleading basis for choosing massing, since manipulations facilitating performance during training can reduce the quality of learning.
requirements: Quizzes administered on a schedule that permits distributing questions on an objective across at least three quizzes spaced weeks apart
Use of algorithmic question variants so repeated questions differ only in superficial features
constraints: Practice-quiz scores will be lower in the short term, which matters when quizzes are credit-bearing; the decrement falls mainly on the first two questions on an objective
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in calculus courses
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of objective-specific calculus knowledge
examples: In the study, three algorithmic variants of each objective's question appeared either all on the first quiz after introduction (massed) or one per quiz across three consecutive quizzes (spaced), with the criterial test counting toward course grades

article_title: Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap
citation: Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2024). Navigating Spatial Ability for Mathematics Education: a Review and Roadmap. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09935-5
title: Three-family taxonomy of spatial ability structures: specific-factor, broad-factor, and unitary
description: The review organizes the sprawling spatial ability literature into three general types of taxonomies. Specific-factor structures use factor-analytic methods to identify subcomponents such as spatial orientation, mental rotation, and non-rotational spatial visualization; broad-factor structures use theoretically motivated categories such as large- versus small-scale or the intrinsic-extrinsic by static-dynamic 2x2; unitary structures treat spatial ability as a single factor. The review states these were chosen "to highlight the main sub-factor dissociations in the literature" and to make definitions navigable for non-specialist mathematics education researchers.
requirements: Researchers selecting a taxonomy must match it to the data collected and the theoretical framework of the inquiry, since the review states a taxonomy shapes interpretation and generalization of findings.
constraints: The review states the three-type account is not comprehensive, and that no validated instruments exist for the broad-factor or unitary taxonomies.
target_learners: mathematics education researchers and practitioners selecting spatial measures
target_learning_goals: measuring and theorizing spatial ability as it relates to mathematics learning
examples: The review details exemplar dissociations within the specific-factor family, such as spatial orientation versus rotational spatial visualization, and mental rotation versus non-rotational spatial visualization.

article_title: Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education
citation: Sofia Tancredi, Dor Abrahamson. (2024). Stimming as Thinking: a Critical Reevaluation of Self-Stimulatory Behavior as an Epistemic Resource for Inclusive Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09904-y
title: SpEED: special education embodied design framework for inclusive embodied instruction
description: SpEED is a design-based research framework for inclusive design grounded in embodied cognition, introduced in prior work by the first author and applied here to analyze how instructional designs privilege sensory modalities. The article explains that "SpEED differentiates the sensory and motor systems engaged, such as vision (modality), materials, such as printed textbooks (media), and system of meaning making, such as diagrams and language (semiotic mode) of instructional designs and highlights their interrelation." SpEED names modalism as the privileging of a dominant modality (e.g., vision in geometry teaching) that makes content less accessible to learners with different sensory access, and calls for instruction rooted in the modalities through which a learner explores the world. Its principles hold that learning happens through sensorimotor engagement, begins from learners' existing embodied resources, and must flexibly adapt to sensorimotor diversity.
requirements: Instruction must flexibly adapt to learners' sensorimotor diversities and build from learners' existing embodied resources
constraints: The framework diagnoses exclusionary design (e.g., oculocentric geometry instruction) rather than inherent learner pathology
target_learning_goals: disciplinary concepts such as geometry accessible through non-dominant modalities
equitable access to embodied sense-making
examples: The article uses SpEED parameters to analyze the Balance Board Math design, which leverages the vestibular modality commonly engaged in stimming but uncommonly engaged in learning contexts

article_title: Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention
citation: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005
title: Simultaneity account of gesture's effect on learning: temporal synchrony between speech and gesture enables integration of complementary messages
description: The article advances an account in which instructor gesture promotes durable, generalizable learning because it conveys a complementary message simultaneously with speech, allowing learners to integrate two strategies across modalities. The authors write that "speech and gesture appeared to encourage learners to simultaneously attend to and integrate ideas conveyed in the two modalities and thus create long-lasting and flexible new concepts." This account is framed within dual-channel theories of multimedia learning and the Contiguity Principle, and is contrasted with an embodied-cognition account in which gesture's bodily origin alone would suffice. The experiment supports the simultaneity account because sequential cross-modal presentation conferred no advantage over speech alone.

The gesture must be interpretable within the context provided by concurrent speech
constraints: The account concerns instructor-produced gesture watched by learners; the authors note it may not extend to self-produced gesture
The design did not test gesture-first sequencing or algorithm-in-speech/principle-in-gesture combinations
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural understanding of mathematical equivalence
generalization to novel problem formats
retention over delays
examples: Third graders solved missing-addend problems (e.g., 4+3+7=__+7) after instruction pairing the Equalizer principle in speech with the Add-Subtract algorithm in gesture, simultaneously or sequentially

citation: Gehlbach, H., Mascio, B., & McIntyre, J. (2021). Social perspective taking: A professional development induction to improve teacher-student relationships and student learning. Journal of Educational Psychology (in press). https://osf.io/suhvj/
title: Six-step social perspective taking induction for teachers with a focal student
description: A 90-minute professional development induction in which "teachers progressed through the social perspective taking induction steps with a partner, concentrating on the focal student whose behavior they found perplexing." examples: Treatment teachers completed the induction at a central location in November, then recorded hypotheses and proposed action steps for their focal student

article_title: Shall we teach spelling by rule?
citation: Cook, W. A. (1917). Shall we teach spelling by rule? The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Shall+we+teach+spelling+by+rule%22
title: If spelling rules are taught at all, they must be introduced in the elementary school during the habit-forming period and given in widely-separated doses
description: This principle states the author's concluding recommendation about when and how spelling rules may profitably be taught. He argues that rules "do not teach themselves", that they "cannot be taught once and then dismissed from attention like an event in history", and that "they must be introduced, if at all, in the elementary school during the habit-forming period, while the pupil still spells reflectively rather than automatically". It is drawn from his test results rather than from a tested manipulation.
requirements: Teachers must insist upon the rules being learned and give them in widely-separated doses for thoroughness of digestion.
constraints: The author states the presumption is against a favorable outcome even under these conditions, except with a superior teacher.
target_learners: elementary school pupils in the habit-forming period
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of common words in written discourse
examples: University freshmen and academy students taught the rules the previous winter or six weeks before the test largely failed to recall or profit from them.

The authors confirm there is "sufficient information for an independent researcher to reproduce all of the reported methodology". These shared instruments support replication and reuse by other researchers studying social perspective taking in teacher professional development.
requirements: Hosting in a public, open-access repository that preserves the materials in a time-stamped, immutable, permanent format
target_learners: teachers participating in the professional development induction
target_learning_goals: measuring teacher-student relationships and student learning outcomes
examples: Two OSF repository links are printed in the disclosure: one for student measures and one for teacher measures

article_title: The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes.
citation: Poffenberger, A. T., Jr. (1915). The influence of improvement in one simple mental process upon other related processes. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(8), 459-474.
title: Specific stimulus-response bonds and identical elements as the mechanism of transfer of training
description: The article explains transfer through Thorndikean bonds between situation and response: improvement spreads only when the two tasks share identical elements or when one process incorporates bonds previously formed. "This test seems to indicate that learning is facilitated by incorporating into the process to be learned previously formed bonds between situation and response, or, in other words, it indicates the transfer of identical elements." Interference arises when a new response to the same stimulus requires breaking an old bond. The experiment was designed to isolate these specific bonds by eliminating general factors such as adaptation to the experimental conditions.
requirements: Tasks must be analyzable into stimulus and response components so that identical or conflicting bonds can be identified
constraints: The authors note it will probably never be possible to analyze any process into stimulus and response terms within the nervous system, where any real transfer must finally be located
target_learners: adult subjects familiar with psychological tests
target_learning_goals: efficiency of simple mental processes such as naming, cancellation, and arithmetic operations
examples: The seven test comparisons varied the relation between training and test processes from close similarity to complete antagonism

article_title: The influence of speed drills upon the rate and the effectiveness of silent reading.
citation: Peters, C. C. (1916). The Influence of Speed Drills Upon the Rate and the Effectiveness of Silent Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Give speed drills as a regular part of the teaching of reading
description: The article recommends incorporating speed drills into reading teaching, on the grounds that its seven-month experiment showed a relative improvement of 18.7% in speed without injuriously affecting quality. The drills used easy, interesting narrative matter, occupied five to ten minutes of the reading period, and paired silent reading under speed exhortation with oral reproduction checked by questioning to guard against skimming.
requirements: Drills must use relatively easy, interesting narrative reading matter
Oral reproduction with questioning must accompany the drills as a guarantee against skimming
Total reading time must not exceed that given to comparison instruction
constraints: The experiment did not confirm that speed increase carries effectiveness increase within a given individual
Comparisons between groups under different teachers and buildings were not ideal for experiment
target_learners: elementary school pupils in grades three to six
target_learning_goals: increase silent reading speed while maintaining comprehension quality
examples: In the Royersford experiment, drill groups read easy narrative silently with the exhortation to see who could finish first, then a pupil told the substance of what was read and was questioned on omissions.

article_title: The effect of practice upon visualizing and upon the reproduction of visual impressions.
citation: Foster, W. S. (1910). The Effect of Practice upon Visualizing and upon the Reproduction of Visual Impressions. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Formal training in visualizing and visual reproduction has limited general value; specific practice is demanded for best results and becomes quickly effective.
description: The article concludes that "the value of formal training of our kind had been greatly overestimated", because little ability is gained by continuing practice beyond a relatively short time and gains are specific to identical ability-conditioning factors. It recommends specific practice targeted at the exact material and conditions rather than general formal visualizing exercises.
requirements: Practice must be matched to the specific material, time, instructions and conditions under which the ability is to be used.
constraints: Conclusions were drawn from adults already trained in habits of attentive observation; the authors state they have no right to extend them wholesale to immature or untrained persons.
target_learning_goals: reproduction of briefly exposed visual material from memory
examples: Three observers practiced reproduction of dots, polygons, nonsense figures, pictures and objects across about thirty series; gains concentrated in the first half of practice and did not transfer across material kinds.

article_title: Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress.
citation: Peters, W. (1912). Pedagogy at the Berlin Psychological Congress. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 3, 452-457. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Pedagogy+at+the+Berlin+Psychological+Congress
title: Spearman's theory of general intelligence, defended against the similarity theory and the type theory
description: In his address on general mental capacity, Spearman distinguished three theories of the relations of single mental abilities: "The similarity theory, which assumes that high correlation exists only between those activities which are very similar; the type theory, which affirms that correlation of mental abilities is a function of certain types, and Spearman's own theory of 'general intelligence.'" He critically examined the literature of the past 32 years and endeavored to demonstrate in it the presence of a general intelligence factor, also including physiological data favorable to his contention. The report presents this as a defense of general intelligence as distinct from special abilities.
requirements: Demonstration rests on critical re-examination of the existing correlation literature plus physiological data.
target_learning_goals: understanding and measurement of general mental capacity versus special aptitudes
examples: Spearman's congress address critically examined 32 years of literature to argue for a general intelligence factor, alongside Stern's report defending general intelligence as distinct from special abilities.

article_title: Self-regulated spacing in a massive open online course is related to better learning
citation: Paulo F. Carvalho, Faria Sana and Veronica X. Yan. (2020). Self-regulated spacing in a massive open online course is related to better learning. npj Science of Learning 5:2. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0061-1
title: Use spaced study as a buffer that improves performance for lower-ability students and those who do not engage in active practice
description: This principle holds that distributing study across multiple sessions offers an alternative route to the benefits of active practice: "for those students who do not engage in as many activities during learning, they can instead space out their learning more to obtain the same benefits". The article frames spacing as working "as a buffer, improving performance for low ability students and those who do not engage in active practices". It applies to self-regulated online and course-based learning where learners control their own study schedules.
requirements: Learners must have the opportunity to return to the same unit content across multiple study sessions separated in time.
constraints: The evidence is observational, so a third variable such as motivation cannot be eliminated; those who neither space nor complete activities are likely to underperform.
target_learners: MOOC and online course students, including lower-ability students and students who complete few practice activities
target_learning_goals: Retention and quiz/exam performance of complex course material such as introductory psychology
examples: In the MOOC data, spacing was defined as the number of sessions students took to complete a unit, averaging 4.08 sessions per unit, and more sessions related to higher quiz grades within the same student.
