article_title: Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory
citation: Vanessa Frei & Nathalie Giroud. (2025). Immersive auditory-cognitive training improves speech-in-noise perception in older adults with varying hearing and working memory. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00306-5
title: Speech-memory paradigm: a short-term auditory-cognitive training with natural continuous speech and varying memory load, in audio-only and immersive stereoscopic VR modalities
description: The training element is a speech-memory task in which participants hear natural continuous sentences with varying memory loads (one vs two sentences, 60 items per session) and answer a verbal comprehension question after each item. As the article describes it, "The AU and IM approach used the same training task and consisted of a speech-memory task, whereby participants were presented with natural continuous sentences with varying memory loads and were required to answer a comprehension question after each sentence." The immersive version presents the speaker via a stereoscopic three-dimensional 180-degree video in an HP Reverb G2 head-mounted display; sessions lasted about 40-45 minutes, and comprehension questions after high-load items always referred to the first heard sentence, with mock items every tenth trial to prevent listening strategies.
requirements: Natural continuous speech material presented at a normalized 70 dB level with comprehension questions to enforce processing
Randomized item order and single presentation of each item to reduce repetition-based learning effects
constraints: The immersive environment predominantly increased redundant sensory information given the very favorable listening situation, per the authors' interpretation; perceived immersion was not systematically assessed
target_learners: healthy older adults (61-80) with mild to moderate hearing loss and varying cognitive capacities
target_learning_goals: speech comprehension of natural continuous speech
selective attention and working memory engagement during listening
examples: Each session contained 30 low-load (one-sentence) and 30 high-load (two-sentence) items on general-knowledge topics such as Flora, Fauna, and Swiss History, spoken by a trained actress who was also the visualized speaker

article_title: Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage?
citation: Wickliffe C. Abraham, Owen D. Jones and David L. Glanzman. (2019). Is plasticity of synapses the mechanism of long-term memory storage? npj Science of Learning 4:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0048-y
title: The synaptic plasticity and memory (SPM) hypothesis holds that experience-dependent synaptic change is a fundamental mechanism of learning and memory retention
description: The SPM hypothesis proposes that memories are stored primarily through experience-dependent changes at synapses. The review describes how this concept gained sway after electrophysiological work revealed lasting activity-dependent synaptic changes such as LTP and LTD. Martin et al.'s four evidentiary criteria (detectability, mimicry, anterograde intervention, retrograde intervention) are presented as the framework for confirming it. The review concludes the hypothesis has strong support but lacks conclusive proof that memories reside at synapses.
requirements: Confirming the hypothesis requires evidence meeting Martin et al.'s criteria: detectability, mimicry, anterograde intervention, and retrograde intervention
constraints: The review states we are still without conclusive proof that memories reside at synapses, and non-synaptic mechanisms have emerged that are also capable of acting as memory substrates
target_learners: learners across species studied in memory research (mammals and invertebrates)
target_learning_goals: long-term memory storage and retention
examples: The review cites detectability of synaptic plasticity after many forms of learning and reversal learning inducing complementary reversal of synaptic plasticity

article_title: An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts
citation: Luke McCrone & Martyn Kingsbury. (2024). An ecological approach to understanding transitions and tensions in complex learning contexts. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00267-1
title: A taxonomy of spatial, pedagogic and agentic transitions and tensions between formal and informal learning spaces
description: The article defines three categories of transitions and tensions between timetabled and non-timetabled learning spaces. 'Spatial' ones "exist as a function of timetables and architectural divides between formal and informal space"; 'pedagogic' ones exist between teacher-centred transmission intent and student-centred intent, producing 'failed', hidden and postponed interactions; and 'agentic' ones occur between the fixed power dynamic of the lecture theatre and the more democratic adjacent informal space. The taxonomy emerged from mixed-methods analysis of occupancy data, ethnographic observation and field interviews, and conceptualises the spaces as interconnected ecological zones.
requirements: Requires mixed-methods data combining quantitative occupancy monitoring with ethnographic observation and field interviews to detect the transitions and tensions
constraints: Derived from one lecture theatre and adjacent breakout space in a UK STEM university chemical engineering department
target_learning_goals: supporting active learning
managing transitions between timetabled and non-timetabled learning
examples: Occupancy plots of type 1 and type 2 timetable configurations, sociograms of breakout space interaction, and field interviews with students were used to characterise on-ramp and off-ramp transitions

article_title: Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively
citation: Utkarsh Upadhyay, Graham Lancashire, Christoph Moser and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez. (2021). Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively. npj Science of Learning 6:26. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00105-8
title: Spaced selection framework: optimizing question selection probabilities under an exponential forgetting curve model
description: The article introduces a machine learning modeling framework that, rather than optimizing the rate of study, optimizes which questions to include in each study session. It represents study sessions as triplets of time, question set, and recall vector, models recall probability with the "exponential forgetting curve model with binary recalls", estimates forgetting rates via a variant of half-life regression, and derives optimal selection probabilities p*_i(t) = (1/√q)(1 − m_i(t)) using stochastic optimal control. The resulting procedure is named SELECT.
requirements: Learner review and recall data to estimate forgetting rates via half-life regression
Learners must be tested in each study session, as in the app used
constraints: The parameter q trades off recall probability upon review and study-session size; in the trial the user chose session size, so results are agnostic to q
target_learners: Adult learners (18+) studying large sets of paired-associate items, e.g., driver's permit theory questions
target_learning_goals: Long-term memorization and retention of factual paired-associate content
examples: In the randomized trial, the app presented questions in the order given by the selection probability while the user chose the size of the study session.

article_title: Does splitting sleep improve long-term memory in chronically sleep deprived adolescents?
citation: Cousins, J. N., van Rijn, E., Ong, J. L., Wong, K. F., & Chee, M. W. L. (2019). Does splitting sleep improve long-term memory in chronically sleep deprived adolescents? npj Science of Learning 4:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0047-z
title: For chronically sleep-restricted learners, scheduling a daytime nap as part of a split sleep schedule can harness afternoon learning without impairing morning learning
description: This principle holds that when adolescents cannot obtain adequate nocturnal sleep, dividing the available sleep between a shortened night and a mid-afternoon nap supports memory better than concentrating the same total sleep at night, particularly for afternoon learning. The article states that "a split sleep schedule appears to be preferable for harnessing the cognitive functions that underpin learning in the afternoon, without negatively impacting upon morning learning", and that "facilitating naps in schools may be an effective measure to improve learning outcomes". It is grounded in the experimental comparison of split versus continuous restricted sleep on picture encoding and factual knowledge.
requirements: A mid-afternoon nap opportunity (1.5 h in the study, chosen to allow a full cycle of N2, SWS and REM sleep) in addition to nocturnal sleep
constraints: The evidence applies under sleep restriction below the recommended 8–10 h; whether splitting sleep advantages adolescents with adequate habitual sleep was not tested
The 90-min nap "is toward the upper limits of nap durations that may be practical to implement in schools"; shorter naps of 30–60 min have shown benefits but were not tested in this schedule
Splitting sleep reduced total sleep time and REM sleep, and REM-linked faculties (procedural memory, creative problem solving, emotional regulation) may have been affected
target_learning_goals: Long-term memory for school learning material encoded across the school day (factual knowledge and picture recognition)
examples: In the simulated school week, the split group's 1.5 h nap at 14:00–15:30 followed afternoon learning blocks about amphibian species, and the group remembered more of that material after recovery sleep

article_title: Evidence for a unitary structure of spatial cognition beyond general intelligence
citation: Malanchini, M., Rimfeld, K., Shakeshaft, N. G., McMillan, A., Schofield, K. L., Rodic, M., Rossi, V., Kovas, Y., Dale, P. S., Tucker-Drob, E. M. & Plomin, R. (2020). Evidence for a unitary structure of spatial cognition beyond general intelligence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0067-8
title: Spatial Spy: a gamified virtual-reality battery assessing six spatial orientation skills
description: Spatial Spy is a novel gamified online battery set in a virtual city, developed in Unity by ETT Solutions, assessing six spatial orientation skills: map reading, route memory, navigation by directions, navigation by landmarks, large-scale scanning and large-scale perspective taking. Participants "solve a mystery by collecting clues while orienting and navigating around the streets of a virtual environment". Tasks combine accuracy and reaction-time scores equally weighted; the battery took 35–60 minutes (median 43) and was validated in 2,660 TEDS twins.
requirements: A web browser on a desktop or laptop computer with mouse or trackpad and keyboard; a training session and practice trials precede testing
constraints: Assessment in a computer-simulated environment may capture spatial orientation less well than real-life settings; the authors propose VR orientation may reflect an allocentric approximation of egocentric real-life orientation
target_learning_goals: spatial orientation and navigation skills (map reading, route memory, wayfinding, scanning, perspective taking)
examples: TEDS twins completed the battery online in web browsers, pausing with the 'P' key; test–retest reliability was estimated in a 100-participant pilot completing the battery twice over two months

article_title: Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students
citation: Zanchi, P., Mullier, E., Fornari, E., Guerrier de Dumast, P., Alemán-Gómez, Y., Ledoux, J.-B., Beaty, R., Hagmann, P., & Denervaud, S. (2024). Differences in spatiotemporal brain network dynamics of Montessori and traditionally schooled students. npj Science of Learning, 9, 45. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00254-6
title: The spatiotemporal connectome framework characterizes brain dynamics via system diversity (integration) and spatiotemporal diversity (stability)
description: The spatiotemporal connectome is an analytical framework that characterizes resting-state functional connectivity with a structural prior: neural activity is chunked into time windows, connectivity matrices (506 × 506 regions) constrained by structural connectivity are translated into connected components (CCs), and CCs are classified by the eight functional systems of Yeo's atlas plus the cerebellar system. From these, two group-level metrics are derived: "system diversity (SD) and spatiotemporal diversity (STD)", where SD informs about "integration and segregation" and STD about "temporal stability". The article uses these metrics to compare Montessori- and traditionally schooled students at global and functional-system scales.
requirements: SD and STD require a sufficient number of connected components for a reliable outcome, so they are computed at group level rather than individually
constraints: SD and STD are group-level measures, which prevents correlating brain metrics with individual behavioral measures in this study
target_learners: students aged 4 to 18 in Montessori or traditional schools
target_learning_goals: characterizing how pedagogical experience relates to brain network integration and temporal stability
examples: The article applied the framework to 87 students' resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI, comparing SD and STD at global and functional-system scales between pedagogy groups.

citation: Katie A. Gilligan-Lee, Zachary C. K. Hawes and Kelly S. Mix. (2022). Spatial thinking as the missing piece in mathematics curricula. npj Science of Learning 7:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00128-9
title: Spatial visualization skills taxonomy: mental rotation, mental transformation, perspective taking, and spatial scaling
description: The article organizes target spatial skills under the umbrella of spatial visualization, defined as "the ability to generate and mentally manipulate objects or images". As shown in its Fig. 1, activities targeting spatial visualization include mental rotation (mentally turning objects/shapes by degrees of rotation), mental transformation (mentally combining or deconstructing shapes within or across planes), perspective taking (imagining scenes from different points of view), and spatial scaling (mentally mapping between spaces of different scales). constraints: The article notes these activities are seldom referenced in mathematics curricula and none are mentioned in the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

using spatial visualization as a mental blackboard to model and manipulate mathematical problems and relations

description: The article recommends keeping existing shape and measurement curriculum strands and using them as entry points for spatial thinking, rather than eliminating them. citation: Alalawi, K., Athauda, R., & Chiong, R. (2024). It lets academics generate course-specific predictive models from historical continuous assessment data, run predictions after each assessment, identify at-risk students via dashboards, and deliver personalised interventions. The article states that "SPPA is implemented as a web application and is accessible by course instructors (also called academics in this paper) and students via a web browser." It integrates pedagogical principles such as constructive alignment and Hattie and Timperley's feedback model, and is released as an open-source project.

constraints: Prediction and intervention are only possible after students submit at least the first continuous assessment task

improved pass rates and grades through targeted interventions
examples: Deployed in six courses at a tertiary institution with four academics piloting learning analytics interventions

citation: Rebecka Weegar · Peter Idestam-Almquist. (2024). Reducing Workload in Short Answer Grading Using Machine Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00322-1
title: Modular spreadsheet-based grading setup combining clustering, sampled manual grading, classification, and full review

title: Assess internal consistency of AI-based scores by splitting input text into comparable parts and correlating part scores
description: This principle recommends dividing the input text into two or more parts of comparable length, obtaining an AI-based score for each part, and calculating a measure of stability between the part scores as an estimate of internal consistency. target_learning_goals: reliable automated scoring of written work
examples: In the empirical example, each text was split into two parts with similar or equal numbers of sentences, and Yule's Q was calculated with analytical confidence intervals

description: The article frames the spacing effect as an explanatory account of why distributed practice improves retention, noting that "the mechanisms underlying the consolidation of long-term memory remain a topic of ongoing research, with multiple hypotheses coexisting." title: Standardized Patient Simulation-Based Pedagogy (SPSP) package embedded with lecture for teaching MSE
description: The SPSP package is a four-week training combining MSE lectures with standardized patient simulation in a skills laboratory. Per Table 1, SPSP materials included "pictures, scenarios, problem-based questions", delivered via "Gallery work, each one teaches one, group discussion, pictorial method, and simulation", with 15-minute SP interviews followed by 10-minute structured debriefing in groups of 5 to 8 students. Trained standardized patients portrayed signs and symptoms of mental illness across MSE domains, and students rotated through nurse and observer roles.
requirements: Trained and rehearsed standardized actors who can retain scenario scripts and portray MSE symptom domains
A skills laboratory with semi-cycle seating and MSE checklists for students
Trained research trainers facilitating sessions of 120 minutes, three sessions per week
constraints: The study did not show the separate effect of the lecture embedded in the SPSP training materials
SPs did not portray all symptom domains, since portraying all symptoms might exaggerate those of a real patient
target_learners: Diploma nursing students in middle college (ages 16–32)
target_learning_goals: Mental status evaluation cognition: concept, content and implementation of MSE for identifying mental illness
examples: In the study, the intervention group interviewed an SP portraying abusive language, over-talkativeness, delusions and hearing voices, while controls learned via lectures and real patients without mental illness symptoms in general medical wards
key_sources: Singano Violeth E., Millanzi Walter C., Moshi Fabiola. (2024). Effect of standardized patient simulation-based pedagogics embedded with lecture in enhancing mental status evaluation cognition among nursing students in Tanzania: A longitudinal quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05562-4

title: Use a spiral curriculum that iteratively revisits basic science topics from undergraduate through postgraduate training to reinforce and integrate knowledge
description: The article recommends that basic sciences revision continue beyond the early undergraduate years, because some early concepts may not be fully reinforced. Medical educators "should consider the use of a spiral curriculum which involves iterative revisiting of topics with each encounter building on the previous knowledge", which the authors say will enhance deep learning, reinforce prior knowledge and stimulate knowledge integration. This addresses the retention decline documented after graduation.
requirements: Curricula must better integrate basic sciences with clinical practice from undergraduate to postgraduate training years
constraints: The recommendation is argued from the study's findings and cited literature rather than tested directly in this study
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of basic science knowledge
deep learning and knowledge integration
examples: The article cites evidence that continuous engagement through clinical practice, continued education and teaching enhances knowledge retention

article_title: [Communication training in otorhinolaryngology education : Comparison of an online and a classroom-based training course].
citation: Gür Deniz, Offergeld Christian, Fabry Götz, Wünsch Alexander. (2024). Vermittlung kommunikativer Kompetenzen in der Lehre der HNO-Heilkunde: Vergleich zwischen einer Online- und Präsenzveranstaltung. HNO. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00106-024-01475-2
title: COM-ON-Check observation framework grounded in the SPIKES six-step bad-news protocol with the NURSE emotion-handling model integrated
description: The article structures its observer feedback tasks around a named assessment framework: the COM-ON-Check Rating Scale, which the article states is "theoretisch auf dem SPIKES-Modell zur Übermittlung schlechter Nachrichten aufgebaut". SPIKES comprises six steps (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Strategy and Summary) for structuring difficult conversations. The NURSE model of Back et al. is integrated into the observation tasks to guide handling of emotions: Naming, Understanding, Respecting, Supporting, Exploring. In this study these frameworks operationalize what peer observers watch for during simulated consultations and what feedback the practising student receives.
requirements: Trained simulated patients and tutors who can apply the observation tasks
Observer assignments distributed to the non-practising students in each group
constraints: Applied here specifically to an otolaryngology scenario involving a hearing-impaired patient and cochlear implant counselling
target_learning_goals: Structuring clinical conversations, delivering difficult news, and responding appropriately to patient emotions
examples: Observation tasks include items such as greeting, avoiding background noise, keeping eye contact, speaking slowly, making pauses, and not shouting
